hints: Look at the states given, from gas for fluorine and chlorine to solid for iodine, and think what this tells you about how easily each element forms a vapour.
walkthrough:
Link state to volatility**
Think of volatility as how easily a substance escapes into the gas phase. Fluorine and chlorine are already gases at room temperature, so they escape very easily. Iodine is a solid, so it hardly escapes at all.

State the trend clearly**
Going from gas to liquid to solid down the group means it becomes harder to form vapour. So you can say with confidence that volatility decreases down Group 17.
Final answer: Volatility decreases down Group 17.

hints: Identify the only intermolecular force between non-polar diatomic halogen molecules like $\text{Cl}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$.
Think how the number of electrons per molecule changes from fluorine to iodine and how this affects the strength of temporary dipoles.
walkthrough:
See what has to be broken**
When a halogen boils, you are not breaking the strong $\text{X-X}$ covalent bond inside the molecule. You are only separating one $\text{X}_2$ molecule from its neighbours. The attractions to overcome are induced dipole-dipole forces, also called London dispersion forces.

Why the forces get stronger**
Down the group each molecule has many more electrons, for example $\text{Cl}_2$ has 34 electrons while $\text{I}_2$ has 106. A larger electron cloud is more easily distorted, so stronger temporary dipoles form. That means stronger attractions between molecules.

Connect to volatility**
Stronger attractions need more thermal energy to break apart, so boiling point increases. A higher boiling point means the element vaporises less readily, so volatility decreases.

Final answer: Down the group the number of electrons per molecule increases.
This causes stronger induced dipole-dipole (London dispersion) forces between molecules, so more energy is needed to separate them and volatility decreases.

hints: Recall that a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide from solution, so decide which species is oxidised and which is reduced.
walkthrough:
Spot the displacement pattern**
Chlorine sits above iodine in Group 17 and is the stronger oxidising agent. That means $\text{Cl}_2$ will take electrons from $\text{I}^-$ and force iodine out as $\text{I}_2$.

Write the balanced equation**
You need two $\text{I}^-$ ions to make one $\text{I}_2$, and two $\text{Na}^+$ ions to pair with the two $\text{Cl}^-$ ions formed. This gives $$\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{NaI} \rightarrow 2\text{NaCl} + \text{I}_2$$

hints: Recall the classic colours for silver halides, white for chloride moving through cream for bromide to yellow for iodide.
Remember that solubility in ammonia decreases down the halide group, so chloride dissolves most easily.
Distinguish between no visible change for the least soluble precipitate and dissolving in excess ammonia for the more soluble one.
walkthrough:
Picture the two precipitates**
Adding $\text{Ag}^+$ to halide ions gives $\text{AgX}(s)$. For iodide you get a distinctly yellow solid, silver iodide $\text{AgI}$. For chloride you get a white solid, silver chloride $\text{AgCl}$. Colour alone already distinguishes them.

Use ammonia as the confirmatory test**
Excess aqueous $\text{NH}_3$ forms a soluble complex with silver. $\text{AgCl}$ is soluble enough to dissolve completely in excess dilute ammonia. $\text{AgI}$ is far too insoluble, so there is no visible change.

Fill the table carefully**
For $\text{NaI}$: colour yellow, name silver iodide, effect of excess ammonia no change. For $\text{NaCl}$: colour white, name silver chloride, effect of excess ammonia dissolves.

Final answer: $\text{NaI}(aq) + \text{AgNO}_3(aq)$: yellow precipitate of silver iodide, $\text{AgI}$, no visible change with excess aqueous ammonia.
$\text{NaCl}(aq) + \text{AgNO}_3(aq)$: white precipitate of silver chloride, $\text{AgCl}$, dissolves in excess aqueous ammonia to give a colourless solution.

hints: Focus only on the ions that combine to make the solid, and leave out $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{NO}_3^-$ which stay in solution.
walkthrough:
Cancel the spectators**
In full, $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{NO}_3^-$ appear on both sides and do nothing. The real change is $\text{Ag}^+$ meeting $\text{I}^-$ to form solid $\text{AgI}$.

Add correct states**
Both ions start in aqueous solution and the product is a solid precipitate, so write $$\text{Ag}^{+}(aq) + \text{I}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgI}(s)$$

hints: Think what type of reaction gives only $\text{HCl}(g)$ from $\text{NaCl}$, with no change in oxidation number of sulfur or chlorine.
Look at the products $\text{I}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ from $\text{NaI}$ and decide what has been oxidised and what has been reduced.
Compare the reducing strength of $\text{I}^-$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ to explain why sulfuric acid can oxidise one but not the other.
walkthrough:
The NaCl case is simple acid behaviour**
With chloride, you just get proton transfer to make hydrogen chloride gas: $$\text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4 + \text{HCl}$$ No oxidation numbers change, so sulfuric acid is acting only as an acid.

The NaI case involves redox**
With iodide you still make $\text{HI}$ at first, but then $\text{HI}$ is oxidised to purple $\text{I}_2$ fumes while sulfur in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is reduced from +6 down to -2 in $\text{H}_2\text{S}$. Here sulfuric acid is acting as an oxidising agent and $\text{I}^-$ is acting as a reducing agent.

Explain the difference**
Iodide is a much stronger reducing agent than chloride because its outer electron is further from the nucleus and lost more easily. Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is strong enough to oxidise $\text{I}^-$ but not strong enough to oxidise $\text{Cl}^-$. That is why $\text{NaCl}$ gives only $\text{HCl}$ while $\text{NaI}$ gives further oxidised products.

Final answer: With $\text{NaCl}$, concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ acts only as an acid, e.g. $\text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4 + \text{HCl}$.
With $\text{NaI}$, concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ acts as an oxidising agent, oxidising $\text{I}^-$ to $\text{I}_2$ while itself reduced to $\text{H}_2\text{S}$.
$\text{I}^-$ is a more powerful reducing agent than $\text{Cl}^-$, so $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ can oxidise $\text{I}^-$ but not $\text{Cl}^-$.

hints: Think in terms of electrons, if the agent oxidises something else, what must happen to the agent itself.
walkthrough:
Use the electron picture**
Oxidation of one species always goes with reduction of another. An oxidising agent forces another species to lose electrons, and to do that it must pick those electrons up itself. So an oxidising agent is a species that gains electrons.
Final answer: An oxidising agent gains electrons (is an electron acceptor, is itself reduced).

hints: Remember chlorine reacts with water to give two acids, $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{HClO}$, with no other reactants needed.
walkthrough:
Build the two acid products**
One chlorine atom picks up hydrogen and oxygen to become chloric(I) acid, $\text{HClO}$, the useful disinfectant. The other becomes hydrochloric acid, $\text{HCl}$. Balancing atoms gives $$\text{Cl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{HCl} + \text{HClO}$$

hints: Recall that hot aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ gives chlorate(V), $\text{NaClO}_3$, not chlorate(I), so balance $\text{Cl}_2$ with $\text{NaOH}$ to make $\text{NaCl}$, $\text{NaClO}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Assign the oxidation number of chlorine in $\text{Cl}_2$, in $\text{Cl}^-$ and in $\text{ClO}_3^-$ to show both an increase and a decrease.
walkthrough:
Write the correct hot alkali equation**
Cold $\text{NaOH}$ would give $\text{NaClO}$, but hot conditions push oxidation further to chlorate(V). The balanced equation is $$3\text{Cl}_2 + 6\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 5\text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check it: 6 Cl, 6 Na, 6 O and 6 H on each side.

Track oxidation numbers to prove redox**
In $\text{Cl}_2$ each Cl is 0. In $\text{NaCl}$ Cl is -1, a decrease, so reduction. In $\text{NaClO}_3$, with 3 O at -2 each and Na at +1, Cl must be +5, an increase, so oxidation. Because the same element is both oxidised and reduced, this is a disproportionation redox reaction.

Final answer: $3\text{Cl}_2 + 6\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 5\text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$
Chlorine oxidation number changes from 0 in $\text{Cl}_2$ to -1 in $\text{NaCl}$ and +5 in $\text{NaClO}_3$; chlorine is both oxidised and reduced, so this is disproportionation and therefore redox.
